analysis.one_liner: Creates a pilot program funding local job guarantees that offer a job to anyone who applies in high-unemployment areas.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in February 2026 with 2 cosponsors, was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat with no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have the Labor Department give competitive grants to local governments, Tribal entities, and similar bodies in areas with high unemployment — at most 15 of them — to run job guarantee programs. Anyone in the area who applies would be offered a job paying at least the prevailing wage or the local minimum, with health coverage comparable to federal employees' insurance, paid family leave, and paid sick time. Grants would last up to 3 years, and an independent evaluation would measure the pilot's effects on employment, poverty, health, and incarceration rates. The bill also expands the Work Opportunity Tax Credit so employers get a tax break for hiring people who spent at least 3 months in a job guarantee program.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of high-unemployment communities — places where local unemployment is at least 1.5 times the national rate, including Tribal areas — would be the direct beneficiaries: any adult in a pilot site could get a job with a solid wage floor, union-scale protections, and federal-employee-grade health coverage. Workers in those areas benefit from a rule barring the program jobs from displacing existing employees, and unemployed residents gain training, child care, transportation, and reentry support to help them move into other work. Employers who hire program graduates would get an expanded Work Opportunity Tax Credit.

how_it_helps.text: Local governments in high-unemployment areas would get grants to create jobs available on demand to residents 18 and older, with a wage set at the greater of the FLSA-determined rate (as if a higher minimum wage law were in effect), the state or local minimum, the local prevailing wage, or the applicable union contract rate [S2].
Participants would get health insurance comparable to what federal employees receive, plus paid family leave and paid sick time [S2].

Grant funds could also pay for supportive services — transportation, child care, dependent care, housing — plus training, adult education and literacy, reentry support for people with criminal records, and financial literacy help [S2].
The jobs could not displace existing workers or undercut union contracts, and program jobs would be placed in existing bargaining units where similarly situated workers are represented [S2].
Federal agencies would be asked to make some of their own jobs available to participants, with the Labor Department reimbursing agencies' full costs [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the pilot, with appropriations left open-ended ("such sums as may be necessary") and grants capped at 15 sites for 3 years. Low-wage employers in pilot areas would face competition for workers from jobs paying at least the prevailing wage with health benefits. Grantees would bear audit and reporting costs, with funds clawed back if misused.

drawbacks.text: The bill is written as a small pilot limited to at most 15 grantees for 3 years, so it would not create a federal job guarantee nationally — only test one in a handful of high-unemployment areas [S2].

The federal government would pay an open-ended amount: the appropriations section funds "such sums as may be necessary," and the evaluation section requires comparing program costs against reduced public-assistance and other federal spending in the area, an implicit requirement that savings offset the program's cost [S2].
The wage floor references an as-yet-unenacted minimum wage bill (S. 2823 of the 119th Congress) as if it were law, so actual participant wages would depend on legislation that has not passed [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit would be significant for the residents of the hardest-hit communities: a real job offer to anyone who wants one, with federal-standard wages and health benefits, in areas where private employers have not created enough work. The main costs are fiscal and design-related: as a pilot it covers only 15 areas rather than the whole country, its full cost is open-ended ("such sums as may be necessary"), and its evaluation requires it to pay for itself through reduced public assistance and other savings — a bar a small pilot may struggle to meet. But the drawbacks that matter most here are procedural: with 3 cosponsors and no movement in the Finance Committee, its chance of becoming law in this Congress is low.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat ever since — no hearings, no vote, no movement.

narrative.text: Senator Booker introduced S. 3864 on February 12, 2026 [S1] [S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, the customary first step for a tax-and-spending bill [S4].
The action history shows no committee hearings, no markup, and no floor vote since the referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill only got as far as a committee referral, nothing has changed for anyone yet; the outcome so far simply preserves the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; status quo holds

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on February 12, 2026.

sides.party_line_note: All three supporters are Democrats; no Republican senators cosponsored, and the bill went to the Senate Finance Committee, which has taken no action on it.

industries.industry: State and local governments in high-unemployment areas
industries.note: They would receive federal grants to run job programs and gain a workforce for public services, but must supply matching state, local, or philanthropic support and pass annual audits with clawbacks for misused funds [S2].

The pilot guarantees jobs paying at least the prevailing wage with federal-employee-grade health benefits, which would compete with employers who pay less; there is also an explicit anti-displacement rule barring grantees from replacing existing private-sector jobs [S2].

The bill protects union contracts and places program jobs into existing bargaining units, but also caps public works jobs so they cannot displace union-represented positions — protective on both sides of the ledger [S2].

analysis.trajectory: The bill has sat in the Senate Finance Committee since its February 2026 referral with no hearings, markup, or vote, and only 2 cosponsors. Bills at this stage with this level of support rarely advance; unless the committee schedules action, the bill will likely die when this Congress ends in January 2027.
